newsitem.title: USA: New York legislators salvage rent laws.
newsitem.headline: New York legislators salvage rent laws.

text.p: New York's rent-control regulations were saved from extinction early Monday morning as state lawmakers hammered out a deal in last-minute negotiations, a press spokesmen said.

The three key players involved -- Gov. George Pataki, Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno and Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver -- met a "conceptual agreement" at about 12:30 a.m. EDT, scrapping plans for a 30-day extension of the laws, which govern 1.2 million apartments and 2.7 million New Yorkers, primarily in New York City.

"They are still working out the details of a conceptual agreement. They all agreed on a broad outline and details will be decided. They intend to pass a bill sometime later on Monday," Charles Carrier, spokesman for Assembly Speaker Silver, said.
Silver declined to release details on what the new deal specified, but said legislators were working through the night on the new deal.

The rent laws, in force for 50 years, set limits on what landlords can charge tenants in pre-World War II buildings; rent stabilization affects apartments in buildings built before 1974. The laws were intended to create a larger pool of housing for low and middle-income renters.

Landlords complain the laws prevent their charging market value, allowing well-heeled tenants to rent sprawling apartments at low prices, but supporters of rent-control say the laws have prevented New York City from becoming a city only for the wealthy.
The rent-control laws technically expired at midnight.

Pataki issued an executive order Saturday to set up a 24-hour hotline to handle calls from tenants concerned about their fate. By Sunday night, more than 1,400 phone calls from worried tenants had been placed to the hotline. He also designated New York State Attorney General Dennis Vacco as special prosecutor to protect tenants from dishonest landlords.
On Sunday, New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani said tenants would not face immediate eviction but he was unclear about their fate if the laws were allowed to lapse.

Pataki and Bruno, both upstate Republicans, pushed for rent decontrol of apartments once a tenant dies or move out. Under the plan, rent control was available for senior citizens and the disabled and the broad rights of succession for family members and loved ones to a rent-controlled apartment were maintained.
Silver, a Manhattan Democrat, contended that partial decontrol will eventually curb rent laws for all apartments and leave tenants at the mercy of greedy landlords.
The mood of negotiations at the state Capitol building where state leaders worked on the agreement was quiet despite the recent fervor surrounding the debate.

As lawmakers decided their fate, a few dozen tenants held a candlelight vigil outside the Capitol. Their numbers were low compared to the several hundred tenants organizers had expected to descend on Albany to protest the end of rent control in New York, one of the last states to continue with a housing practice started after World War II.
